client: I've been really stressed out lately because I missed the deadline for my final project at university, and I just can't stop thinking about how badly it's going to affect my grade. Every time I try to sit down and work on it now, I just freeze up and my mind goes blank with worry. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the damage is already done.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — the worry about your grade is understandable, and that freeze response when you sit down to work makes a lot of sense when your mind is so flooded with "what ifs." I also hear a bit of hopelessness in the idea that talking won't help, and I want to gently challenge that — while the deadline has passed, how you move forward from here is still very much in your hands. What thoughts tend to run through your mind the moment you sit down to work on the project — what's the first thing that shows up?

client: The first thing that shows up is this voice that says "you've already ruined it, so what's the point." It's like before I even open the document, I've already decided the outcome is going to be bad, and then I just... sit there feeling sick to my stomach. I know that sounds kind of irrational when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: It's actually a really meaningful moment that you noticed it sounds irrational when you say it out loud — that gap between what the thought *feels* like and what it *actually is* is exactly where we can do some useful work together. That voice saying "you've already ruined it" is what we'd call an automatic thought, and it's jumping to a conclusion before you even have any real evidence of the final outcome. If a close friend came to you in this exact situation — missed deadline, still able to submit — what would you actually tell them about whether it's worth trying?

client: I mean... I'd probably tell a friend to just submit it anyway, that something is better than nothing. But it feels different when it's me — like I can already picture my professor's face, or the way my classmates would judge me if they found out I was late. I know logically that's not the same as actual evidence, but the feeling is so strong it's hard to separate it from what's real.
therapist: You've actually just done something really insightful — you gave yourself the same advice you'd give a friend, *and* you recognized that the images of your professor and classmates are your mind filling in the blanks, not actual evidence of what will happen. That tendency to treat a vivid mental image as if it's a confirmed reality is so common, and it makes sense that it feels hard to shake even when you can see it logically. I'm curious — if you imagine actually submitting the project, even late, what's the most realistic outcome you can picture, separate from the worst-case story your mind is telling you?

client: I mean... if I'm being honest, the most realistic outcome is probably that my professor just accepts it with a late penalty and moves on, because they have like a hundred other students to deal with. But even knowing that, there's still this knot in my stomach that won't go away, like my body hasn't gotten the memo that the catastrophe probably isn't coming. It's frustrating because I can think it through logically and still feel just as anxious as before.
therapist: What you're describing — your mind and body being out of sync — is actually one of the most frustrating but normal parts of anxiety, and it doesn't mean your logical thinking isn't working. That knot in your stomach is like an alarm system that got triggered and hasn't quite gotten the "all clear" signal yet, even though your rational mind has already done the hard work of reality-checking the situation. One thing that can help bridge that gap is taking the action your logical self already knows makes sense — submitting the project — because sometimes the body only starts to calm down once it sees the evidence that things are okay. What feels like the smallest possible first step you could take toward opening that document today?

client: I hear what you're saying, and the alarm system metaphor actually makes some sense to me. But honestly, the idea of opening that document right now makes my stomach drop even more, like just looking at it will make everything feel more real and more terrifying. I guess the smallest step might be just... opening my laptop, but even saying that out loud feels ridiculous because it's such a tiny thing and I'm still dreading it.
therapist: It doesn't sound ridiculous at all — it actually shows a lot of self-awareness to recognize that opening the laptop *is* the real threshold right now, and that tiny steps are exactly how we move through dread rather than around it. The fact that something feels small on the outside but huge on the inside is a sign of how much emotional weight you've attached to this situation, not a sign that you're being irrational or weak. What do you think it would feel like on the other side of that moment — once the laptop is open and nothing catastrophic has immediately happened?

client: Honestly, I think there'd be this brief moment of relief, like "okay, I didn't die" — but then I'd probably just be sitting there staring at all the unopened emails and feeling that dread creep back in. It's like I can imagine the relief lasting maybe five seconds before the actual problem is right in front of me again. So part of me wonders if opening the laptop just trades one kind of dread for another.
therapist: That five seconds of relief you described is actually more important than it might seem — it's proof that your nervous system *can* settle, even briefly, and that's something we can build on rather than dismiss. You're right that opening the laptop trades one dread for another in a way, but there's a difference between dreading something unknown and facing something concrete, because concrete problems are actually the ones we can take action on. What if instead of opening all those emails at once, you gave yourself permission to just open the document and write one single sentence — no more — just to prove to that alarm system that the catastrophe still isn't coming?

client: I hear what you're saying, and the "one sentence" thing sounds simple enough in theory, but I already know what's going to happen — I'll open the document, see how little I've written, and then the guilt about how long I've avoided it will just hit me all at once. It's like the document itself has become this record of everything I've failed to do, and one sentence isn't going to erase that. I want to believe it could work, but I'm not sure I trust that my brain will actually stop at one sentence instead of spiraling.
therapist: It sounds like the document has become something bigger than just a file — it's turned into a symbol of all your self-criticism, which means opening it feels less like a task and more like facing a verdict on yourself. That's a really important thing to notice, because it means the hard part isn't really the writing — it's the story you're expecting the document to tell you about who you are. What would it look like to separate those two things — the actual task of adding words to a page, versus the meaning you've attached to what's already there?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it intellectually — like, yes, it's just words on a page. But when I actually try to separate them in my head, I can't seem to do it, because the whole reason I started that document was to prove something to myself, so the two things feel completely fused together. How do you even begin to untangle that when the meaning was baked in from the very start?
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can see how deeply fused those two things are — the task and what it means about you — because that fusion didn't happen by accident; it sounds like this project carried a lot of personal weight even before the deadline became an issue. Untangling them isn't about convincing yourself the meaning doesn't exist, but rather gently asking: *who decided* that this document gets to be the measure of your worth, and is that a rule you'd apply to anyone else you care about? I'm curious — what were you originally trying to prove to yourself when you started it, and where did that pressure come from?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think I started it wanting to prove I actually belong in this role, that I'm not just someone who got lucky and is faking their way through. The pressure came from... I don't know, maybe from always feeling like I have to justify my place somewhere, like I'm one mistake away from people realizing I'm not as capable as they thought.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — underneath the stress about a deadline, there's this much older and deeper fear that you don't truly belong, and that one mistake will expose you. That's an incredibly heavy thing to carry, and it makes so much sense that this project became so loaded, because it was never really just about the project. I want to sit with that for a moment — where do you think that feeling of "I'm one mistake away from being found out" first came from for you?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. I think it goes back to when I was pretty young, maybe around eight or nine, and my dad would get really quiet and disappointed whenever I brought home anything less than perfect grades. It wasn't like he yelled or anything, but that silence felt worse somehow, like I had to keep proving I deserved to be in the family.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it makes so much sense that a child who learned that silence meant disappointment would grow into someone who feels constantly on the edge of not being enough. That quiet withdrawal from your dad was a powerful message — not because it was true, but because you were young and you needed his approval to feel safe, so your mind built a rule around it that you've been carrying ever since. I'm wondering — when you imagine that eight or nine year old bringing home an imperfect grade, what do you feel toward them?
